title: The Gang Buys a Roller Rink

jokes.text: Charlie rollerskating in the present — 'Look at those moves. You got the moves, Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Three grown men are arguing about Joni Mitchell / Janis Joplin indoors
jokes.punchline: Charlie is apparently already rollerskating while this mundane conversation is happening — the visual absurdity of it lands as a reaction beat before anyone acknowledges it
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP visual absurdity — Charlie skating around during a mundane argument is funny precisely because nobody finds it weird. Character-specific (of course Charlie is doing this) and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why would you deliver such sad news in such an upbeat fashion?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Uh, yeah, you know what? It felt wrong as I was doing it. Wasn't sure how to stop.

jokes.text: 'Why are we doing it?' / 'Oh, South Philly Skate's closing, man.' — delivered upbeat while delivering terrible news
jokes.setup: Mac is dancing excitedly and says the roller rink is closing
jokes.punchline: Dennis: 'Why would you deliver such sad news in such an upbeat fashion?'
jokes.explanation: Tight structure — the juxtaposition of mood and content is a classic comedic mismatch, and Dennis's articulate calling-out of it is well-phrased. 'Why would you deliver such sad news in such an upbeat fashion?' is a genuinely quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Everybody wants to pave paradise and put up a parking lot.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Nice! Nice. Uh, Joni Mitchell, yeah. I found a way to weave it in. I heard you do that.

jokes.text: 'It felt wrong as I was doing it. Wasn't sure how to stop.'
jokes.setup: Dennis calls out Mac's tonal mismatch in delivering bad news cheerfully
jokes.punchline: Mac's explanation — he knew it was wrong but couldn't course-correct — is both a perfect character beat and an absurdly relatable human moment
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. Mac's self-aware helplessness is perfectly phrased — it's funny because it captures a universal awkward experience with specific, unfiltered honesty. Strong economy score (10 words, maximum payoff). Genuinely quotable.

dialogue.line: Hotdogging happens at the concession stand.

jokes.text: 'Everybody wants to pave paradise and put up a parking lot.'
jokes.setup: The gang is devastated about the roller rink closing
jokes.punchline: Mac quotes Joni Mitchell — the artist he was just praising in the argument — as if it's his own profound wisdom, while completely missing the self-referential irony
jokes.explanation: A quick callback that pays off the opening argument by having Mac deploy the Joni Mitchell lyric as his own philosophical observation. The rewatch bonus is real because viewers catch the full circularity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: This jacket's phat as hell.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It may be phat, but you're not supposed to wear it, all right?

jokes.text: 'Nice! Nice. Uh, Joni Mitchell, yeah. I found a way to weave it in. I heard you do that.'
jokes.setup: Mac is pleased with himself for quoting Joni Mitchell
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly acknowledges that Mac was conspicuously trying to work in a Joni Mitchell reference — calling out the artifice immediately deflates Mac's self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: The meta acknowledgment that Mac was 'weaving it in' is a sharp, economical deflation joke. Dennis's immediate call-out lands because the smugness was palpable. Good straight-man beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I got to look phat 'cause I'm out there selling weed, and you got to look phat if you're selling weed.

jokes.text: The gang immediately jumps to 'You want to buy a roller rink?' — 'Oh, God, no. No, no, no. We already tried that.' — cutting to 1998 flashback
jokes.setup: In the present, the gang is figuring out what to do about the roller rink closing
jokes.punchline: The show immediately flashes back to 1998, revealing this entire episode is the origin story of how they accidentally bought a bar instead of a roller rink — a structural meta-joke for longtime viewers
jokes.explanation: The structural joke is excellent — an origin-story episode for a long-running show about terrible people, revealing how they accidentally ended up with their bar. 'We already tried that' is a perfect setup for the entire episode's premise. This is high-concept episode construction, not just a line joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: And also, dude, I'm gonna say this as your friend and not just your boss... stop dealing drugs at work, okay?

jokes.text: 'Hotdogging happens at the concession stand.' — Smokey's roller rink PA announcement
jokes.setup: Smokey is doing a PA announcement telling kids not to hotdog on the rink
jokes.punchline: 'Hotdogging happens at the concession stand' — the literalization of the slang term into a food item is a crisp wordplay joke delivered with total authority
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical wordplay with a great deadpan delivery context. Smokey using the PA to announce this feels both authoritative and absurd. 'Hotdogging happens at the concession stand' is quotable precisely because of its confident literalness.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You know, Dennis looks like Jerry Seinfeld.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Thanks, man. Yeah, that's kind of what I was going for.

jokes.text: "Richie Keen, keep it clean, buddy" — Smokey rhymes the skater's name into his rule enforcement
jokes.setup: Smokey is commanding the rink with earnest authority
jokes.punchline: He rhymes the kid's name as if this is a natural part of management — 'Richie Keen, keep it clean' — delivered without any awareness that it's funny
jokes.explanation: Light wordplay gag. Works because Smokey doesn't acknowledge the rhyme at all — it's just how he runs his rink. Character-specific and efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I don't like how mean they are to each other on that show.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Aw, Sweet Dee. So pure of heart. You know?

jokes.text: 'It may be phat, but you're not supposed to wear it.'
jokes.setup: Mac defends his jacket as 'phat as hell'
jokes.punchline: Dennis concedes it is in fact phat — accepting Mac's premise — while still delivering the correction. The acknowledgment of its phat-ness before the 'but' is the joke
jokes.explanation: The concession 'it may be phat' is a small but effective comedic choice — Dennis doesn't dispute the aesthetic judgment, only the workplace policy. Period slang deployed well.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, no, Charlie, uh, size 11 in men's.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's okay. Oh, right. You wear men's. Yeah. I totally forgot.

jokes.text: 'I got to look phat 'cause I'm out there selling weed, and you got to look phat if you're selling weed.'
jokes.setup: Mac is defending why he needs to wear the jacket at work
jokes.punchline: The justification pivots to drug dealing — which is both a non-sequitur and completely in-character. The circular logic ('you got to look phat if you're selling weed') stated as self-evident truth is the core joke
jokes.explanation: Mac's drug-dealing confidence delivered as workplace professionalism is funny and character-specific. The tautological logic ('look phat... because you're selling weed') is a good absurdist beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Guys, thank you so much for not making fun of the size of her feet. They're—they're very big.

jokes.text: 'Also, dude, I'm gonna say this as your friend and not just your boss... stop dealing drugs at work.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is managing Mac at the roller rink
jokes.punchline: The formal HR-style framing ('as your friend and not just your boss') applied to telling someone to stop dealing drugs is a perfect tonal mismatch — treating a criminal behavior as a minor workplace infraction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-constructed jokes. The setup-to-punchline structure is tight: the professional HR preamble ('as your friend and not just your boss') builds false gravity, then the punchline ('stop dealing drugs at work') lands as a perfect tonal crash. The joke is structurally excellent and very quotable. Close to the 8.0 anchor benchmark — it's sharp, economical, and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mark my words, nobody will ever use email. The Internet is a fad for nerds.

jokes.text: Young Dennis's father tells him to leave his 'cellular telephone on' — 'You work for me now. Yes, Father.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is dropping his kids off to skate; his father gives him orders
jokes.punchline: Dennis robotically responding 'Yes, Father' to a condescending father figure prefigures his control issues and daddy issues that are central to his adult character — but played here as a nervy, subordinate teen
jokes.explanation: Character seeding for Dennis's psychology — his stiff 'Yes, Father' obedience to a dismissive dad is rich context for his later narcissism. More of a dramatic beat with comedic undertones than a pure laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Like, what kind of business is he in?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's complicated, you know? There's—there's numbers and money, you know?

jokes.text: 'You know, Dennis looks like Jerry Seinfeld.' 'Thanks, man. Yeah, that's kind of what I was going for.'
jokes.setup: Dennis shows up to the roller rink in a college jacket
jokes.punchline: Dennis is told he looks like Jerry Seinfeld and takes it as a compliment he was deliberately aiming for — absurd vanity combined with meta-comedy (they're inside a TV show, Seinfeld is a real TV show)
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke of Dennis Reynolds being told he looks like Jerry Seinfeld in 1998, and accepting it as deliberate, is both a good character joke (Dennis's vanity is astronomical) and a clever meta-reference. The deadpan 'that's kind of what I was going for' is the killer beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I definitely see myself running this place one day.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'll be running a multi-million-dollar business, and you'll be working at a roller rink.

jokes.text: 'I don't like how mean they are to each other on that show.' / 'Aw, Sweet Dee. So pure of heart.'
jokes.setup: Mac compares Dennis to Jerry Seinfeld; Dee complains about how mean the characters on Seinfeld are to each other
jokes.punchline: The irony is devastating — Dee is the character who will spend the next 15 seasons being mercilessly mocked by her friends. Mac calling her 'pure of heart' plays perfectly against what the audience knows
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The irony is structural and profound — Dee complaining about Seinfeld characters being mean to each other, while she is about to spend decades being the Gang's punching bag, is pitch-perfect dark comedy. Mac's 'So pure of heart' caps it with devastating sincerity. This earns its high scores: it only works in THIS show, with THIS character, and requires the audience's foreknowledge. The earned_vs_cheap score is 9 because the irony is completely organic — nothing is forced. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mobile phones. Fads for yuppies. Mark my words, Charlie, those things will never catch on.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis enthusiastically encourage Dee to pursue Hollywood: 'You're gonna do great out there, sis. They're gonna love you. You just have so much natural charisma, and you're so funny.'
jokes.setup: Dee announces she's leaving for Hollywood tomorrow — this is set in 1998
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Dee never makes it. The sincerity of Mac and Dennis's encouragement is an unintentional long-form cruelty — they're sending her to fail without knowing it
jokes.explanation: Dark structural irony — the Gang is uncharacteristically kind to Dee precisely because they don't yet know what terrible people they'll become, and the audience knows her Hollywood dreams will amount to nothing. The warmth is the cruelty. Excellent for rewatchers.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Also, you keep saying that, and I don't know if you're, like, fully expecting me to, like, mark these words down 'cause I don't have, like, a pen on me.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis privately congratulate each other for 'not making fun of the size of her feet. They're very big.'
jokes.setup: Dee leaves to skate; Mac and Dennis speak privately
jokes.punchline: They immediately discuss her comically large feet the second she's gone — their self-congratulation for restraint is immediately undercut by doing the exact thing they were praised for not doing
jokes.explanation: Tight ironic structure — 'thank you so much for not making fun of the size of her feet. They're very big.' The act of thanking each other for restraint IS the lack of restraint. Good character work showing early-Gang hypocrisy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: How am I supposed to learn if you don't show me how to do it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You don't know how?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No. I don't know anything.

jokes.text: 'Mark my words, nobody will ever use email. The Internet is a fad for nerds.'
jokes.setup: Smokey is giving Dennis an email address in 1998
jokes.punchline: Mac confidently dismisses the internet as a nerd fad — the dramatic irony of the 1998 setting makes this a period-piece joke about bad predictions
jokes.explanation: Classic '90s period-piece joke — Mac confidently dismissing email is an earned cheap laugh from dramatic irony. The 'fad for nerds' framing is the extra twist. Functional but not particularly original in this genre of comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I thought this was something you'd learn in school.

jokes.text: "There's there's numbers and money, you know?" — Dennis's elaboration on what his dad's business involves
jokes.setup: Pressed on what 'business' means, Dennis tries to elaborate
jokes.punchline: His elaboration is "numbers and money" — the most generic possible description that tells us absolutely nothing, confirming he has no idea
jokes.explanation: Escalation of joke 16 — the follow-up explanation being 'numbers and money' (i.e., the definition of all commerce) is the perfect deepening of the original joke. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I feel like I just watched you have sex with a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah. Why?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What do you mean why?

jokes.text: "I definitely see myself running this place one day." / "Dooley, come on, man. No headlocks!" — Charlie's corporate ladder ambitions interrupted by rink management
jokes.setup: Charlie is making his case for why he's climbing the corporate ladder, paralleling Dennis's claim about running his dad's company
jokes.punchline: He's immediately interrupted mid-speech by having to yell at a kid doing headlocks — his 'corporate ladder' is a roller rink, and his authority is managing children
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom structure — big claim deflated by immediate reality check. The timing of Smokey's interruption (or Charlie's own interruption of himself) is what makes it work. Good visual comedy implied: mid-inspirational-speech, pivot to screaming at children.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It was your idea.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I didn't want to watch you have sex.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I didn't want you to watch me have sex, either.

jokes.text: "You're talking about thumbing through vending machines for loose change. You think that's comparable to my thing?" / "Well, that one's empty, but yeah, you never know."
jokes.setup: Dennis has just called out Charlie's vending machine logic
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response — checking the specific machine he referenced and noting it's empty but remaining optimistic — is the perfect escalation, suggesting this is a regular practice and he has a system
jokes.explanation: This escalation is excellent. Charlie actually physically checks the machine mid-argument, finds it empty, and STILL defends the premise with 'you never know' — this confirms he does this regularly and genuinely believes it has merit. It's not just a dumb joke, it's a character revelation. The specificity ('that one's empty') elevates it from generic-dimwit to precise-Charlie-dimwit.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't even know what it is I'm being fired from.

jokes.text: Dennis's father says 'Ah, my special little helper' and then clarifies he meant his pill, not Dennis: 'Oh, not you. I was talking about this little guy.'
jokes.setup: Dennis arrives with his father's briefcase; father greets him warmly
jokes.punchline: The warm greeting is not for Dennis — it's for a pill. The callous dismissal of his son in favor of a performance-enhancement drug is both funny and genuinely dark, foreshadowing Dennis's psychological damage
jokes.explanation: Strong misdirection with real darkness underneath. The reveal that 'my special little helper' refers to a pill rather than his son is structurally clean and character-defining. Dennis's father openly preferring a Viagra-adjacent pill over his son is both funny and genuinely revealing about Dennis's upbringing. The 'Right here' pointing to the pill is a great visual beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I just sold two ounces of Compton Endo.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Holy shit. Whoa, dude, there's got to be, like, $80 in there.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's $4,000, Charlie.

jokes.text: 'It enhances my performance and impresses my colleague, if you know what I'm saying?'
jokes.setup: Dennis's father is taking mystery pills at the roller rink, about to have a 'meeting'
jokes.punchline: The 'if you know what I'm saying' nudge signals it's a performance-enhancement drug for sex — casually delivered to his teenage son
jokes.explanation: The delivery to his own son is what makes it dark — it's functional setup for the larger joke about to come (Dennis watching his father have sex). On its own, it's a broad hint, not a full joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, got to tighten them Dee's nuts. / Dee's nuts.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm sorry. I just don't find crass humor that funny.

jokes.text: Dennis asks to 'sit in the corner and watch' his father's work meeting; father says 'that's a little weird'
jokes.setup: Dennis wants to learn his father's business by watching; asks if he can sit in and observe
jokes.punchline: The dialogue is a double entendre — Dennis genuinely means business; his father hears 'watch me have sex with a prostitute.' The miscommunication is the cringe engine.
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP miscommunication cringe — the double meaning is carefully constructed so both readings are completely plausible. 'I could just sit in the corner and watch' / 'How am I supposed to learn if you don't show me?' lands perfectly because neither party knows they're having different conversations. Strong rewatch value as the irony compounds on second viewing.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Cool? Charlie, in 20 years, everybody's gonna have a beeper. Mark my words.

jokes.text: 'Honey.' / 'Yeah, what I'm saying is Silly String's not so silly when it's stuck in a wheel bearing.'
jokes.setup: Cut to Smokey in the middle of an apparently unrelated conversation in the rink
jokes.punchline: The completely non-sequitur statement about Silly String and wheel bearings, delivered mid-conversation with total authority, is a perfect absurdist cutaway — 'So, actions do have consequences. You know?'
jokes.explanation: Absurdist non-sequitur delivered with Smokey's characteristic gravity. 'Silly String's not so silly when it's stuck in a wheel bearing' is a great absurdist aphorism. The pivot to 'Actions do have consequences' as a philosophical conclusion is a perfect Smokey beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Maybe I'll introduce myself, too? Put a name to the face 'cause customer service is important.

jokes.text: "I don't love this, Dennis, but if you want, you can sit in the corner and watch. But no eye contact 'cause that'll throw me off my game."
jokes.setup: Dad has reluctantly agreed to let Dennis observe
jokes.punchline: "No eye contact 'cause that'll throw me off my game" — a performance note that only makes sense if the 'meeting' is a sexual encounter. The specificity of 'throw me off my game' is both funny and horrifying as the reveal approaches.
jokes.explanation: The most explicit pre-reveal clue, delivered as a mundane management note. 'Throw me off my game' applied to what turns out to be sex with a prostitute while his son watches from the corner is peak cringe setup.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: They will return, no matter what, because they're addicted to the drugs.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh. That's how it works. / Oh. Okay, cool.

jokes.text: 'I'm gonna have to sell the joint. Lot of good people are gonna lose their jobs. Kills me, but it's over.'
jokes.setup: Smokey announces he's selling the place — seemingly about the roller rink
jokes.punchline: He's actually talking about the bar, not the rink — which the gang misunderstands. But the gravity of Smokey's delivery ('Kills me, but it's over') applied to what turns out to be a dingy bar is an understatement joke
jokes.explanation: Setup for the episode's central misdirection — Smokey's solemnity about selling 'the joint' is applied to a dump bar. Works better in context of the reveal later.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hi. I'm Charlie. I'll be taking care of you guys this evening.

jokes.text: Young Charlie counting out money: '18, 19. Worth every penny.' — paying $19 for the rink? Or something else?
jokes.setup: Charlie is counting out money with great satisfaction
jokes.punchline: The punchline is implicit — whatever Charlie is spending $19 on with great pride ('worth every penny') is clearly laughably small-time, consistent with his character's perpetual underachievement
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat — Charlie's $19 transaction with great gravitas is consistent with his perpetual small-time nature, but the joke isn't quite defined enough to fully land without the visual context.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm a little thrown off. I was expecting you guys to be so much older than me.

jokes.text: Dennis's father hands Dennis an envelope with '$2,000' — 'There's a little something in there for you.' — to stay quiet about the prostitute
jokes.setup: Dennis has just witnessed his father have sex with a prostitute
jokes.punchline: His father casually bribes him to stay quiet — treating paying off his own son as a mundane business transaction. 'Say hello to your sister' as he walks away is the casual kicker
jokes.explanation: 'Say hello to your sister' as he walks away after paying hush money to his son is a perfect dark casual kicker. Frank's total lack of shame or discomfort is the character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Sorry. It's my first night. I'm in training, so... thank you for your patience.

jokes.text: 'Well, there you go. You happy?' / 'I feel like I just watched you have sex with a prostitute.' / 'Yeah. Why?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is reeling from whatever he just witnessed
jokes.punchline: Dennis's exact description — 'I feel like I just watched you have sex with a prostitute' — and his father's flat 'Yeah. Why?' is devastating. The 'Why?' implies total lack of shame and treats it as a reasonable workplace activity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. 'Yeah. Why?' is an extraordinary two-word response — it confirms Dennis's read AND questions why that's a problem, all with zero defensive energy. The father's total ease with the situation is both funny and deeply revealing about Dennis's upbringing. The structure is clean (statement → confirmation → blank non-comprehension), the character integration is excellent, and 'Yeah. Why?' is genuinely quotable. Comparable in construction quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's a gat. I got a gat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You're carrying around a gun handle?

jokes.text: Full escalating argument: 'It was your idea' / 'I didn't want to watch you have sex' / 'I didn't want you to watch me have sex, either' / 'I thought you were gonna show me what you do at work' / 'This is what I do at work'
jokes.setup: Dennis and his father are both horrified but for different reasons — neither wanted this
jokes.punchline: The parallel structure of mutual disgust ('I didn't want to watch' / 'I didn't want you to watch') while simultaneously affirming the act is work is a perfect comedic escalation
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure works well — each exchange adds a new layer of horror. The parallel 'I didn't want to / I didn't want you to' creates a funny mirror dynamic. 'This is what I do at work' as the final, baffled confirmation is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's still cool, though.

jokes.text: 'Well, I probably would tease you, too.' / 'Yeah, but it's not my fault. You never showed me anything.' / 'I thought this was something you'd learn in school.'
jokes.setup: Dennis laments that the guys teased him about not knowing how to do what his dad does
jokes.punchline: His father's response — 'I thought this was something you'd learn in school' — applied to hiring prostitutes is a spectacular piece of dark comedy parenting. The earnestness makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Genuinely dark and excellent. 'I thought this was something you'd learn in school' as a father's explanation for why he never taught his son to hire prostitutes is both horrifying and hilarious. The character integration is strong — Frank's oblivious sociopathy is perfectly previewed here. The economy is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: All right, well, look on the bright side, Mac. We just made a quick 25 cents.

jokes.text: 'You are officially fired.' / 'What? This is not working out for me, Dennis. You watched me bang, I mean, and now you're whining. You're gonna go cry to your mommy. It's too much.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is upset about witnessing his father with a prostitute
jokes.punchline: 'You watched me bang, I mean' — the father's correction reveals he nearly said something even more crass about his own son, before catching himself. The HR framing ('not working out for me') applied to firing his son for being traumatized
jokes.explanation: 'You watched me bang, I mean' — the stumble and correction is a perfect character beat for Frank. The firing framing is also funny — treating witnessing workplace prostitution as an employee performance issue.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And I'm starting to think that my dad's a bad man.

jokes.text: 'Here's five grand.' / 'What is this?' / 'That's to keep your mouth shut. That's your paycheck.' / 'My sever—' / 'That's your severance pay.'
jokes.setup: Frank fires Dennis and hands him an envelope
jokes.punchline: The rapid reclassification of the same money — hush money, then paycheck, then severance — delivered so fast Dennis can't even finish the word 'severance' before Frank redefines it again, is a great escalating bit
jokes.explanation: Tight escalation joke — Frank relabeling the same money three times in rapid succession while Dennis can barely keep up is well-structured and economical. The interrupted 'My sever—' / 'That's your severance pay' beat has great rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mark my words, you're probably never gonna see that guy again for the rest of your life.

jokes.text: Mac waves drug money: 'I just sold two ounces of Compton Endo.' / Charlie: 'Holy shit.' / Mac: 'Whoa, dude, there's got to be, like, $80 in there.' / Mac: 'It's $4,000, Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Mac flashes a wad of cash from drug dealing
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely wrong estimate ($80 for what is clearly a large stack) followed by Mac's correction ($4,000) captures both Charlie's perpetual financial incompetence and Mac's pride in his drug income
jokes.explanation: Charlie estimating $80 for a large stack of drug money is a great character beat — his financial cluelessness is consistent and specific. Mac's flat correction without breaking stride ('It's $4,000, Charlie') is well-delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What if we went into business, like, for ourselves?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Like we do what Dennis's dad does at work, right, but we do it with each other.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he has a gun: 'That's why I got myself a gat.' — dramatic pause — then shows it to Charlie
jokes.setup: Charlie asks if dealing drugs is dangerous
jokes.punchline: 'Damn straight it is, Charlie. That's why I got myself a gat.' — Mac confirming the danger while also having already acquired a firearm is both a good escalation beat and a character-specific choice
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation — the reveal that Mac has armed himself for his amateur drug dealing operation is consistent with his bravado and sets up the broken-gun payoff later.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: From the machines and my paycheck and just, like, saving the quarters and shit, I've saved up, like, $57,000.

jokes.text: 'Oh, got to tighten them Dee's nuts.' [beat] 'Dee's nuts. They're your nuts, so I said, Dee's nuts. Like...'
jokes.setup: Dee asks Charlie to tighten the axle nuts on her skates
jokes.punchline: Charlie accidentally says 'Dee's nuts' — the accidental deez nuts joke — and immediately tries to explain it straight-facedly, which makes it both more awkward and funnier
jokes.explanation: The 'deez nuts' joke structure applied to the period setting (1998) works well — this joke would have landed differently in-universe since the meme didn't exist yet. Charlie's earnest explanation of why he said it ('they're YOUR nuts, so I said Dee's nuts') is what elevates it from a cheap wordplay gag to a cringe comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: II-When she asked me to tighten her skates, I secretly loosened them, you know, 'cause real friends don't slow each other down, right? They help them soar.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, I'm sorry. I just don't find crass humor that funny.' [reaction beat — Dee's innocence]
jokes.setup: Charlie accidentally makes a 'deez nuts' joke
jokes.punchline: Dee's earnest 'I just don't find crass humor that funny' — from a character who will spend years making and receiving brutal crass insults — is a perfect ironic character beat
jokes.explanation: Excellent character irony — Young Dee's prissy rejection of crass humor, from a person who will become one of TV's most crass and abused characters, is rich with dramatic irony. The specific phrase 'crass humor' has an almost Victorian delicacy that makes it funnier. Strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm fine, you small-haired cunt.

jokes.text: Mac says 'Now I said it' about 'Dee's nuts' after trying to move on from it — 'That happens.'
jokes.setup: Charlie accidentally said 'Dee's nuts'; now Mac accidentally says it too while trying to avoid it
jokes.punchline: 'That happens.' — Charlie's resigned acknowledgment that this is an occupational hazard of her name, delivered with zero embarrassment
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the running gag continues with Mac also falling into the trap. 'That happens' is the perfect Charlie deadpan that implies this is a known recurring issue, not a one-time accident.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: A breath mint 'cause your mouth smells like you just ate a giant slice of shit pizza.

jokes.text: 'Also, you keep saying that, and I don't know if you're, like, fully expecting me to, like, mark these words down 'cause I don't have, like, a pen on me.'
jokes.setup: Mac keeps telling Charlie to 'mark my words' about his predictions
jokes.punchline: Charlie takes 'mark my words' literally — he's been trying to figure out if he's supposed to actually write these down, and has been unable to because he has no pen
jokes.explanation: A great Charlie literalism gag — his earnest concern that he's failing to properly 'mark' the words because he lacks a pen is perfect Charlie logic. The character integration score is high because only Charlie would think this way. Very quotable and delivers a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm gonna get rich, I'm gonna get famous, and I'm probably gonna marry Scott Wolf.

jokes.text: "In 20 years, everybody's gonna have a beeper. Mark my words."
jokes.setup: Mac's beeper goes off; Charlie admires it
jokes.punchline: Mac confidently predicts universal beeper adoption — the wrong technology again, compounding his and Charlie's pattern of confident wrong predictions
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the wrong-tech-prediction running gag. This one is notably worse than the others because beepers were ALREADY being replaced by mobile phones in 1998 — Mac is predicting universal adoption of obsolete technology while holding the obsolete technology. That specificity helps.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Sweet Dee is not being very sweet.

jokes.text: Charlie arrives at the drug deal wearing roller skates: 'Oh, Jesus Christ.' — skating up to buyers
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie to take off his skates before the drug deal; Charlie refuses because he skated to work in socks
jokes.punchline: Charlie literally skates up to the drug dealers — the visual of roller-skating to a drug deal while trying to look intimidating is a perfect physical comedy image
jokes.explanation: The image of Charlie rolling up to a drug deal on skates — after a whole conversation about whether he should — is a great visual comedy beat. 'Oh, Jesus Christ' from Mac is the perfect reaction. Character-specific absurdity at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Smokey
dialogue.line: I don't own this place. I just work here for the free parking.

jokes.text: Charlie introduces himself to drug buyers: 'Hi. I'm Charlie. I'll be taking care of you guys this evening. Uh, uh, how we doing?'
jokes.setup: Mac has told Charlie this is a drug deal; do NOT introduce yourself
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately introduces himself with full hospitality service language, turning a drug deal into a restaurant interaction — having explicitly been told not to do this
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Charlie immediately violating the specific instruction he was just given ('don't introduce yourself') while doing it in the most absurdly service-industry way possible is both funny and perfectly Charlie. 'I'll be taking care of you guys this evening' in a drug deal context is a great line. Character integration 9: only Charlie does this.

dialogue.speaker: Smokey
dialogue.line: I own the bar around the corner.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's a bar around the corner?

dialogue.speaker: Smokey
dialogue.line: Yeah. That place is a real dump.

jokes.text: Charlie counts out bags one by one, drops one, picks it up, apologizes: 'Sorry. It's three, four, five. Sorry. It's my, it's my first night. I'm in training, so... Thank you for your patience.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to execute a drug deal
jokes.punchline: Charlie fumbles the bags like a new restaurant employee — dropping one, recounting, apologizing, explaining he's in training — while thanking the drug buyers for their patience with the service
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest sequences — Charlie's fumbling, apologetic, service-industry approach to a drug deal escalates beautifully. 'Thank you for your patience. I'm in training' is exactly what a new employee says, and the application to drug dealing is both specific and brilliant. Impact 9 — this is the kind of extended cringe sequence IASIP does better than anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We'll take it. Any price.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, well, hang on a second. We don't know if we'll take it. We haven't even seen it yet.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Stop saying that. You are a terrible negotiator.

jokes.text: 'I'm gonna need $40 for— I'm gonna need $40!'
jokes.setup: Charlie is struggling to announce the price of the drugs
jokes.punchline: Charlie can't say '40 for drugs' so he just shouts the number with no context — the price announcement getting louder and more disconnected from any recognizable drug deal protocol is a great escalation
jokes.explanation: Good escalation within the drug deal cringe sequence — Charlie shouting '$40!' with no object is a natural extension of his ineptitude. The build to chaos is well-managed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, there's a palpable sadness in here.

jokes.text: Mac reveals the gun: 'I got a gat.' — buyer examines it — 'Uh, that's the handle. Just the handle.' / 'I can see that. You're carrying around a gun handle?' / 'Yeah, I found it in the trash. It's still cool, though.'
jokes.setup: Mac pulls out his 'gat' to threaten the drug deal that's going sideways
jokes.punchline: The gun is just a handle — no barrel, no mechanism — found in the trash. Mac's insistence that 'it's still cool, though' after being exposed is perfect
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a great callback payoff. The setup (Mac threatening someone with a gat) → reveal (it's just a handle) → explanation ('I found it in the trash') → stubborn defense ('it's still cool, though') is a four-beat escalation that fires on all cylinders. 'It's still cool, though' is an exceptional line — Mac's absolute refusal to concede the point is both funny and deeply character-specific. Excellent economy, strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Guys, mark my words, when we're finished with this place, you're not even gonna recognize it.

jokes.text: 'All right, well, look on the bright side, Mac. We just made a quick 25 cents.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have nearly been shot and their drug deal has fallen apart
jokes.punchline: Charlie's consolation is that they found 25 cents — presumably from the vending machines — immediately after a near-death experience. The tonal mismatch is classic IASIP
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Charlie's earlier mention of collecting quarters from vending machines. The pivot from near-death to '25 cents on the bright side' is a perfect Charlie move — his priorities are always perfectly, obliviously wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I got a lot of things wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah. We really didn't change that much.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You haven't even changed clothes, for instance. You're still wearing the same sweatshirt.

jokes.text: "Mac's a terrible drug dealer, as am I, apparently."
jokes.setup: The gang reconvenes after all three threads (Dennis's dad, Mac's dealing, Charlie's drug deal) have gone wrong
jokes.punchline: Mac includes himself in the failure assessment with a resigned "as am I, apparently" — the 'apparently' suggesting he hadn't previously considered this a failure mode
jokes.explanation: "As am I, apparently" is a good deflating self-assessment. The 'apparently' does a lot of work — suggesting the information is new and somewhat surprising to him.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I learned a lot but I don't really think it's for me.' / 'What is it?' / 'It's complicated, it's messy, and I don't want to describe what I saw.' / '...I'm starting to think my dad's a bad man.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is asked how work with his dad went
jokes.punchline: His description of watching his father have sex with a prostitute as 'complicated' and 'messy' — and his delayed realization that his dad 'might be a bad man' — is a perfect understatement of a deeply weird experience
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan processing of a traumatic event as a workplace dissatisfaction. 'I'm starting to think my dad's a bad man' as the conclusion to watching him hire a prostitute is a great understatement. The word 'starting' is doing a lot of work.

jokes.text: 'You can go your own way. You're your own man. Mark my words, you're probably never gonna see that guy again for the rest of your life.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to encourage Dennis about cutting ties with his terrible father
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Dennis's father is Frank Reynolds — a main character on the show for 15 seasons. 'Probably never gonna see that guy again' is spectacularly wrong in hindsight
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest structural ironies for returning viewers — Mac confidently predicting Dennis will never see his father again, when Frank Reynolds becomes a central cast member. The 'probably' hedge makes it funnier. Very high earned_vs_cheap because this only works in the context of 15 seasons of the show.

jokes.text: 'What if we did what Dennis's dad does at work, but we do it with each other?' / 'You don't want to do what my dad does, okay? And definitely not with each other.'
jokes.setup: Mac suggests they go into business together the way Dennis's dad does
jokes.punchline: Dennis's horrified response — taking Mac's innocuous suggestion as a proposal for group sex work — is a perfect callback double entendre. 'Definitely not with each other' is the killer line
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback double entendre — 'definitely not with each other' is a great line that lands both as a callback to the prostitute scene and as a character beat about Dennis's trauma. The rhythm of 'You don't want to do what my dad does' → 'and definitely not with each other' is excellent. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Charlie reveals he has $57,000 saved entirely from collecting vending machine quarters and his paycheck
jokes.setup: Charlie says he has 25 cents from the machines; asked how much he has total
jokes.punchline: '$57,000' — the reveal that Charlie's obsessive quarter-collecting actually amounts to a significant sum is a great subversion. The specificity of $57,000 (not a round number) is part of the joke
jokes.explanation: Great escalation payoff — Charlie's vending machine quarter obsession, introduced as a joke about his small-time nature, is revealed to have made him the richest of the three. The non-round number ($57,000) makes it feel like a real accumulation, not a made-up figure. Excellent character subversion.

jokes.text: "Oh, dudes, that's perfect. I just got 25 cents, uh, from the machine over there." / "25 cents is not gonna get us shit, man."
jokes.setup: Mac has $4,000, Dennis has $5,000, and they're calculating how to buy the bar
jokes.punchline: Charlie's contribution to the partnership fund is 25 cents — the exact amount from the drug deal aftermath — delivered with the same energy as the thousands
jokes.explanation: Perfect running gag deployment — Charlie's 25 cents from the drug deal aftermath is now his investment capital. The presentation of 25 cents with the same energy as thousands of dollars is classic Charlie. 'No wait, I mean I just got it now. I have more saved up' extends the joke nicely.

jokes.text: 'Equal doesn't quite make sense...' / sandwiches tangent / 'Equal just doesn't totally make sense.' [repeated twice while Charlie is distracted by sandwiches]
jokes.setup: Charlie proposes an equal partnership since he has the most money
jokes.punchline: Dennis keeps quietly trying to establish that equal ownership doesn't make sense — but every time he brings it up, the conversation immediately moves to sandwiches. The repeated deflection is the joke, and sets up the present-day frame where they still haven't resolved it
jokes.explanation: Good running gag — Dennis's repeated attempt to establish unequal ownership being derailed by sandwich logistics is both funny in the moment and sets up a callback to the present-day frame. The issue is apparently NEVER resolved, which is a great running joke for a show called 'It's Always Sunny.'

jokes.text: Charlie secretly loosens Dee's skates instead of tightening them — 'Real friends don't slow each other down. They help them soar.'
jokes.setup: Dee asks Charlie to tighten her skates so she'll slow down for her friends; Charlie nods and says 'positive energy'
jokes.punchline: Charlie LOOSENS the skates on the grounds that true friendship means helping someone go faster — applied logic that is both philosophically generous and immediately catastrophic
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy with a great internal logic — Charlie's act of 'friendship' is to help Dee soar rather than slow her down, which immediately causes her to wipe out. The philosophy ('real friends help them soar') is delivered with total sincerity against immediate physical consequences. 'Help them soar' as a phrase is very quotable. Character integration 8.5 — Charlie's earnest catastrophic helpfulness is core to his character.

jokes.text: Dee wipes out spectacularly on the rink — 'Oh! Oh, shit! Ooh. Goddamn. Ooh. That was brutal.'
jokes.setup: Dee is skating confidently with her friends after Charlie 'tightened' her skates
jokes.punchline: Dee crashes hard; the gang's reactions ('That was brutal') are half horrified, half appreciative
jokes.explanation: The physical payoff to Charlie's skate-tampering. The slapstick is functional — Dee's wipeout is satisfying as a physical gag — but the craft is in the setup, not the fall itself. 'That was brutal' as a spectator comment is good.

jokes.text: Post-crash Dee: 'Yeah, I'm fine, you small-haired cunt.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks if Dee is okay after the fall
jokes.punchline: 'Small-haired cunt' — an absolutely absurd and specific insult that comes from nowhere, delivered as if it's a totally normal response to concern
jokes.explanation: 'Small-haired cunt' is an inspired, specific insult — 'small-haired' is an oddly precise and cutting descriptor that makes no logical sense as an insult but lands anyway because of its confident weirdness. The contrast between Dee's pre-fall sweetness ('I just don't find crass humor that funny') and this explosion is a perfect character reversal. Very quotable. High originality for the specificity of 'small-haired.'

jokes.text: Mac: 'It was a joke, okay? Oh, you don't understand humor?' [defending Dee's insult]
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are shocked by Dee's post-fall insult
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately tries to defend Dee's unhinged outburst as a joke — which calls back directly to Dee's earlier claim that she 'doesn't find crass humor that funny'
jokes.explanation: Decent callback to Dee's earlier declaration, but functions more as a reaction beat following the stronger 'small-haired cunt' joke. Adequate transitional comedy.

jokes.text: 'Hey, Dee, we're gonna buy the rink. Do you want to be part-owner?' / 'Oh, oh, oh, are you?' / 'We could really use your positive attitude.' / 'Oh, oh, oh, could you?'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to invite concussed Dee into the business partnership
jokes.punchline: Dee's rhythmic 'Oh, oh, oh, are you?' / 'Oh, oh, oh, could you?' — clearly still disoriented from the crash — creates a funny pattern of hollow echoing responses while she gathers her rage
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — Charlie's oblivious timing (inviting a concussed person to be a business partner immediately after they wiped out) is funny, and Dee's disoriented echoing responses create a good rhythm before the explosion.

jokes.text: 'You know what you could also use? A breath mint 'cause your mouth smells like you just ate a giant slice of shit pizza.'
jokes.setup: Charlie says they could use Dee's positive attitude
jokes.punchline: 'A giant slice of shit pizza' — the specificity of making it a pizza (not just 'shit') is what elevates this. The image is weirdly precise and disgusting
jokes.explanation: 'Giant slice of shit pizza' is an impressively specific insult — the pizza format, the size, the material. It's gross but specific enough to be genuinely creative. This is Dee as we know her finally emerging. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dee rejects the offer: 'No, Charlie. Thank you, anyway, but I don't want to be involved with you losers, okay? 'Cause you're losers. I'm moving to Hollywood. I'm gonna get rich, I'm gonna get famous, and I'm probably gonna marry Scott Wolf.'
jokes.setup: Charlie invites Dee into the bar business
jokes.punchline: Dee's rejection is a full statement of her 1998 ambitions — including marrying Scott Wolf — all of which the audience knows come to nothing. The specificity of Scott Wolf as the marriage target is perfect 90s period comedy
jokes.explanation: Scott Wolf as Dee's specific celebrity marriage target is a great 1998 period detail — Party of Five-era Scott Wolf is very specific and funny. The cascade of dreams ('rich, famous, probably gonna marry Scott Wolf') building to that specific person is structurally good. The dramatic irony of her future is the dark undertow.

jokes.text: 'Sweet Dee is not being very sweet.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just called Charlie's mouth a 'shit pizza' and stormed off
jokes.punchline: Mac's observation is the most placid possible response to Dee's violent outburst — the understatement is total
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan economy — six words that sum up everything. It's not an original observation (the name irony joke has been done in many shows), but the delivery timing and context make it work well here. High economy score for maximum meaning in minimal words.

jokes.text: 'You know what, man? She just got her bell rung. She's gonna be fine.' — attributing Dee's personality change to the fall
jokes.setup: Dee has just been explosively cruel after a lifetime of sweetness
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis confidently attribute the personality shift to a head injury — not realizing this IS Dee, forever, from now on. They think the cruelty is temporary; the audience knows it's permanent
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes — the guys think Dee's transformation is a temporary concussion effect, but the audience understands this is the moment Sweet Dee became the Dee we know. 'By tomorrow it'll wear off, and she'll be back to spreading her sunshine again' is devastating dramatic irony. The lore-building is elegant.

jokes.text: Gang approaches Smokey about buying 'the rink'; Smokey: 'I don't own this place. I just work here for the free parking.'
jokes.setup: The gang has been treating Smokey as the owner and negotiates to buy 'the rink'
jokes.punchline: Smokey isn't the owner — he's just an employee who works there for the free parking. The entirely misidentified authority figure deflates the whole negotiation
jokes.explanation: 'I just work here for the free parking' is a great character reveal and deflation joke. The gang's entire plan was based on a false assumption about Smokey's status, and his explanation ('free parking') as the entire motivation for being there is both funny and perfectly mundane.

jokes.text: Mac immediately: 'We'll take it. Any price.' / Dennis: 'Well, well, hang on a second. No, we won't pay any price.' / 'We'll pay the appropriate price for a roller rink.'
jokes.setup: Smokey tells them he owns the bar around the corner
jokes.punchline: Mac's immediate capitulation ('any price') followed by Dennis's correction ('the appropriate price') is a great negotiation incompetence beat — their inability to present a united front collapses the deal before it starts
jokes.explanation: Good partner incompetence comedy — Mac and Dennis immediately contradicting each other in a negotiation is both funny and character-true (they can never coordinate). The rhythm of 'any price' → correction → 'appropriate price for a roller rink' is tight.

jokes.text: 'He's a really bad drug dealer, too, man. I can tell.'
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Smokey that Mac is a terrible negotiator
jokes.punchline: Smokey's flat assessment that Mac is also a bad drug dealer — delivered with zero context for how he knows this — is a perfect Smokey non-sequitur delivered with authority
jokes.explanation: 'I can tell' as the entire justification is perfect Smokey energy — total confidence, zero explanation. The callback to the drug deal disaster is implied but Smokey's omniscient assessment lands as a great character beat.

jokes.text: Gang first sees Paddy's: 'Paddy's, huh? You guys like that name?' / 'No. No. No, right? No, it's terrible. It's pretty bad.' / 'We'll change it. Yeah. Definitely. First thing we do.'
jokes.setup: The gang sees the name 'Paddy's' on the bar they're about to buy
jokes.punchline: They all agree the name is terrible and they'll definitely change it — and they never do. 'First thing we do' is the ironic kicker for 15 seasons of never changing the name
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes for returning viewers — the gang confidently planning to change the name 'first thing' and never doing so is a perfect piece of origin-story irony. The unanimity of 'No. No. No, right?' followed by 'First thing we do' is a beautiful comedic construction. Very high rewatch value.

jokes.text: 'Well, there's a palpable sadness in here.' / 'Yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I feel that.' / 'And a stink, right? Like... Yeah. Yeah.'
jokes.setup: The gang enters Paddy's for the first time
jokes.punchline: Their earnest critical assessment of the bar's 'palpable sadness' and 'stink' — which will be its permanent state for 15 seasons — is funny because they're describing the place they're about to enthusiastically buy
jokes.explanation: 'Palpable sadness' as a descriptor for Paddy's is a great phrase — it's accurate about the show's setting and funny because it's identified immediately but ignored. The 'stink' kicker is good. Mostly carries on rewatch irony.

jokes.text: 'We could become really successful bar owners, right? Of course we could, dude. Like, the most successful bar owners in all of South Philadelphia, in all of the country.' / 'That's reasonable.'
jokes.setup: The gang is inspecting the dingy bar and getting excited
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'really successful' to 'in all of the country' — and Charlie's straight 'That's reasonable' — is a great absurdist escalation of their delusional optimism
jokes.explanation: The Gang's signature delusional optimism on full display — 'most successful in all of the country' applied to a bar they just described as having a 'palpable sadness' is classic IASIP irony. 'That's reasonable' as the deadpan kicker from Charlie is well-timed.

jokes.text: Cut to present: bar looks identical to 1998. 'I got a lot of things wrong. Yeah.' / 'We really didn't change that much.' / 'No, you haven't even changed clothes, for instance. You're still wearing the same sweatshirt.'
jokes.setup: 1998 flashback ends; we return to present-day gang in their bar
jokes.punchline: The bar is completely unchanged from 1998. Dennis notes Charlie is literally wearing the same sweatshirt he was wearing in the flashback — the grand plans yielded zero improvement in 20+ years
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural moments — the revelation that nothing changed in 20+ years, underlined by Charlie wearing the SAME SWEATSHIRT, is a perfect summation of the show's entire premise. The gang never grows, never changes, never improves. The specific detail of the sweatshirt is an inspired visual callback. Very high impact for rewatchers who understand the full weight of this.

jokes.text: "I got a lot of things wrong. Yeah." / "Yeah. We really didn't change that much." / "No. No, you haven't even changed clothes, for instance. You're still wearing the same sweatshirt."
jokes.setup: Cut back to the present day — the gang is in Paddy's, now reflecting on the flashback
jokes.punchline: "You haven't even changed clothes" — the bar looks the same, Mac's predictions were all wrong, and Charlie is wearing the same sweatshirt from 1998. The 'sweatshirt' detail as the final indignity confirms the gang's total stasis.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode button on multiple threads simultaneously. Mac's 'I got a lot of things wrong' is a great understated acknowledgment, but 'you haven't even changed clothes' — the visual gag that Charlie's sweatshirt is literally the same as 1998 — is the exceptional detail. It's not just that the bar hasn't changed; it's that Charlie himself hasn't changed, in the most literal possible way. This earns 8+ because it closes multiple arcs (Mac's wrong predictions, the bar's stasis, Charlie's unchanging nature) simultaneously with one visual detail. Structurally very elegant.

jokes.text: Dennis tries to raise the ownership percentage issue in the present; Mac pivots to sandwiches: 'Sandwiches. We were gonna get...' / 'Yeah, we got sandwiches from a place.' / 'Yeah, you hungry? You want a sandwich?'
jokes.setup: In the present, Dennis tries AGAIN to address the ownership percentage issue
jokes.punchline: Twenty-plus years later, the Gang still deflects the ownership conversation with sandwiches — the exact same pattern as 1998. The issue was never resolved
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing structural joke — the ownership dispute still unresolved 20+ years later, still being deflected by sandwiches. The structure score is a 9 because the callback is so precisely constructed: same situation, same deflection, same unresolved outcome. This is the entire show's thesis expressed in a running gag.

jokes.text: 'You're gonna have to pay for it.' — said to Charlie about the sandwich
jokes.setup: The gang offers Charlie a sandwich to distract him from the ownership issue
jokes.punchline: Despite using the sandwich as a deflection to avoid giving Charlie equal ownership, they still make him pay for it
jokes.explanation: Good small cruelty beat — the gang deflects Charlie's ownership claims with a sandwich but still makes him pay, which neatly encapsulates their relationship dynamic. Brief but effective.

jokes.text: Episode ends with Joni Mitchell's 'Big Yellow Taxi' playing over the closing scene — 'They paved paradise, put up a parking lot'
jokes.setup: Mac used the Joni Mitchell lyric at the opening to mourn the roller rink; the episode ends with the song playing
jokes.punchline: The song plays as the gang has essentially 'paved their paradise' (the roller rink dream) to put up a parking lot (a dumpy bar they never improved). The song's thesis is proven about their own story
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural closing — the song that Mac deployed as a philosophical observation turns out to be the thesis of the entire episode. They mourned a roller rink and ended up with a dingy bar. 'They paved paradise, put up a parking lot' is literally what they did to themselves. Good episode-level craft.

tmdb_overview: In the past, an innocent Dennis learns the horrifying details of Frank's business, a truly sweet Dee is excited to head off for Hollywood, while Charlie and Mac's jobs at the roller rink are in jeopardy.
